text: A custom scoped application has run for two years at one department, 150 users, without incident. Now the company plans to roll it out to three more departments over the next year, roughly tripling users and data volume. Leadership asks a Technical Architect for a written readiness assessment: can the platform handle this as configured today, and if not, what has to change first?
At 150 users the application clearly works. A tripling of both users and data volume is a different question entirely, and it's the one the architect has to answer before rollout starts, not after.

Step 1 pulls the core table's schema and checks which fields actually carry an index against the queries its list views and reports really run. A query without an indexed filter can return acceptable results against forty thousand records today and become the next slow list view once that table holds a hundred twenty thousand. A gap found now is cheap to fix; found after rollout, it's a diagnosis.

Step 2 pulls current semaphore and scheduled-job data from the Instance Health Dashboard. At 150 users, utilization sits comfortably below capacity — but the architect projects that number forward. If peak concurrent transactions roughly triple alongside user count, does the pool still have headroom, or is it already close enough to capacity that tripling pushes it into queuing? The architect checks the application's own scheduled jobs the same way, against their maintenance window.

Step 3 is the tracking plan: active users by department as each comes online, record growth on the core table month over month, and peak semaphore utilization, reviewed monthly throughout the twelve-month rollout. A three-times projection usually isn't exactly right. Monthly review is what catches a deviation while there's still time to add capacity or adjust the schedule for the next department.
Table design, semaphore headroom, and a real tracking cadence — one readiness assessment, not three independent checks. Next, Chapter 7 opens with upgrade planning.
